Maren watched them go from the gallery rail, then wound the old clockwork one last time out of habit, though nothing depended on it now.

She still climbed the tower at dusk. There was no lamp to light, but her hands knew the count of the stairs better than they knew her own face in the mirror, and the sea did not seem to have heard that the keeper was retired. She would stand in the lantern room as the beam swung out on its own, steady and indifferent, and the fishing boats would come round the headland below, and she would count them in the way her mother had taught her to count them, one lamp at a time.

She still looked for the boats in the evenings, naming each by the pitch of its engine, and once young Dougal flashed his deck light three times as he passed, which was either habit or kindness, and Maren did not go down to bed.

What surprised her was how the boats kept coming home without anyone to see them in. She had thought herself the light. Now she understood she had mostly been the one who stood at the edge of the land and watched the dark. The sea had never needed her hand on the wick; it had needed someone in the tower who believed each night that the watching mattered.
